name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 11 January 1975

solutions.check: 28 entries, 60 crossings, 0 conflicts, agrees with the 1 answers the paper printed

clue.text: Colourful composer'?'

blocks.note: surface reading: a flamboyant or vivid writer of music
setter's reading: one who colours things, whose job title is also the surname of a Victorian church composer

explanation.walkthrough: Sir John Stainer wrote the Victorian oratorio The Crucifixion; a stainer is someone who applies dye or colour.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of the English church musician doubles as a word for a worker who applies dye to wood or cloth.

clue.text: Good heavens, I've sneezed!

blocks.note: first meaning: an exclamation of surprise
second meaning: the customary blessing a sneezer asks for

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is the blessing one asks for after a sneeze, phrased as the reason for asking.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase serves both as a mild oath of astonishment and as a request for the traditional blessing after a sneeze.

clue.text: Natural thanks might it give for those curds and whey?

definitions.text: Natural thanks might it give for those curds and whey?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone grateful for a simple meal
setter's reading: the meal Little Miss Muffet abandoned when the spider frightened her away, left for the creature to enjoy

explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme a spider sits down beside Miss Muffet and scares her off, so it would have reason to be grateful for her curds and whey.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarantula is a large hairy spider, fitting the creature of the nursery rhyme.

clue.text: Absence of mail-ship standards

blocks.note: no means none, an absence
RMS is Royal Mail Ship, the prefix of British mail steamers

explanation.surface: Without the mail-boat, postal standards slip.
explanation.walkthrough: RMS, Royal Mail Ship, was the prefix of British ocean liners carrying the post.
explanation.definitionFit: Norms are accepted levels or standards of behaviour or performance.

clue.text: Unmanly, according to Donne

blocks.note: surface reading: lacking manliness or courage
setter's reading: John Donne wrote 'No man is an island', so being like an island is, in his terms, not being a man

explanation.walkthrough: Donne's Meditation XVII says 'No man is an island', so anything island-like is, by his logic, un-man-like.
explanation.definitionFit: Insular literally means of or like an island, from Latin insula, the very thing Donne said no man is.

clue.text: Heroic direction, involving both sexes

blocks.note: epic means heroic, as in epic poetry
east-north-east, a compass direction

explanation.surface: A stage instruction for an epic scene with men and women together.
explanation.definitionFit: Epicene describes something with characteristics of male and female, or common to men and women alike.

clue.text: Can one get mean voltage right with this instrument?

indicators.note: the question asks whether one can get these letters into a new shape, working them over into another word

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: An electrician wonders whether this meter will give the correct average voltage.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is close to describing the device in earnest, which hides that its words supply every letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A galvanometer is a meter for detecting and measuring small electric currents.

clue.text: Once a sporting gentleman

blocks.note: surface reading: a man who used to be a sportsman, perhaps now retired
setter's reading: in former times, the word for a gentleman who played sport for love rather than pay

explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' looks like it refers to one man's past; it actually means historically, when unpaid sport was the mark of a gentleman.
explanation.definitionFit: In the nineteenth century the unpaid player was by convention a gentleman, while professionals were working men paid to play.

clue.text: Peter is distressed. Relief needed

indicators.note: something distressed is knocked about and disordered, so the preceding words are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Poor Peter is upset and badly needs some comfort.
explanation.definitionFit: A respite is a short break or rest from something difficult, which is a kind of relief.

clue.text: .Giving favourable consideration to providing hospitality

blocks.note: first meaning: considering an idea or offer seriously
second meaning: having guests and looking after them

explanation.walkthrough: The leading full stop is a printing blemish in the source and plays no part.
explanation.definitionFit: To entertain an idea is to consider it; to entertain guests is to receive and feed them as a host.

clue.text: The archdeacon is attached to meat

blocks.note: an archdeacon is styled the Venerable, abbreviated Ven.
taken as written
something attached is on

explanation.surface: A senior churchman is fond of his roast.
explanation.walkthrough: The Venerable is the title given to an archdeacon in the Church of England, so VEN stands for him.
explanation.definitionFit: Venison is deer flesh eaten as food, one specific kind of meat.

clue.text: Thus a beginner gels an opening, with enough money

blocks.note: thus means so
a learner, as on the L-plate of a learner driver
a vent is an opening that lets air out

explanation.surface: A novice gets a start in business and has money to spare.
explanation.walkthrough: A beginner is L for learner, from the L-plates British learner drivers display.
explanation.definitionFit: Solvent describes someone able to pay their debts, so having sufficient funds.

clue.text: Choice of directions one hears in Oslo

blocks.note: a choice between two compass points

explanation.surface: A choice of routes is offered in the Norwegian capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as N OR SE: two compass points with 'or' between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Norse, the Scandinavian tongue, is the language heard spoken on the streets of the Norwegian capital.

clue.text: Silver named as singular example of this kind of apparel?

definitions.text: Silver named as singular example of this kind of apparel?

blocks.note: surface reading: a garment made of silver thread
setter's reading: the pirate Long John Silver, whose first names make one of the legs of a pair of long johns

explanation.walkthrough: Long John Silver is the pirate of Treasure Island; long johns are long woollen underpants, so a single long john is one example of the garment class.
explanation.definitionFit: Long johns are worn under clothes, so they belong to the general class of garments worn beneath outer clothing.

clue.text: Lady's shoulder-straps came apart? Reprimand

blocks.note: first meaning, whimsical: with its straps broken, her frock falls to the floor
second meaning: to scold someone severely

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful literal reading of the phrase as a garment that has dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone a dressing-down is to rebuke them sharply, so the phrasal verb means to scold.

clue.text: Preserve me, about to give a boy a gun!

indicators.note: about means around, so the pronoun is placed on both sides of the rest

blocks.note: taken as written
to give someone a gun is to arm them; a boy is a lad

explanation.surface: A cry of alarm at the thought of handing a youngster a firearm.
explanation.walkthrough: The M and E wrap around ARM A LAD to make MARMALADE.
explanation.definitionFit: Marmalade is a fruit preserve, usually of oranges, spread on toast.

clue.text: It may be "the cheese for many, excluding etymologists

definitions.text: It may be "the cheese for many, excluding etymologists

blocks.clueFragment: It may be "the cheese for many
blocks.note: surface reading: a popular cheese dish
setter's reading: word historians insist the dish's original name is Welsh rabbit, so only the rest of us use this later spelling

explanation.walkthrough: Welsh rabbit is melted cheese on toast; most people call it Welsh rarebit, a later folk alteration that etymologists reject. The opening quotation mark has lost its partner in the source.
explanation.definitionFit: Rarebit is the popular name for a dish of seasoned melted cheese on toast.

clue.text: Duty List Four, a turn-up for the flier

indicators.note: in a down clue a turn-up flips the pieces so they read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: a rota is a list of duties
IV is four in Roman numerals
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pilot's roster brings a surprise change.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' of 'a turn-up' does double service as the final A of the pieces before the turn.
explanation.definitionFit: An aviator is a pilot, one who flies aircraft.

clue.text: Letter from Greece in water colour

indicators.note: in places one item inside another, so the letter sits inside the body of water

blocks.note: the sea is a body of water
pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A Greek character appears in a watercolour painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'water colour' reads as one art term, but water is the container and colour the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sepia is a reddish-brown pigment and colour, originally made from cuttlefish ink.

clue.text: King Charles, perhaps, may lie uneasily after bridge

indicators.note: lying uneasily means tossing and turning, so the letters shift about

blocks.note: a span is a bridge, or to bridge is to span
taken as written

explanation.surface: The king, restless after a card game, cannot sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King Charles' looks like a monarch; it is the King Charles spaniel, a toy dog breed. 'After' places the jumbled word behind the other piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The King Charles is a breed of small spaniel, so it is an example, flagged by 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Fixed window-pane like Tommy, say?

blocks.note: first meaning: a pane secured in its frame with glazier's putty
second meaning, playful: wearing puttees, the cloth leg-wrappings of the British soldier

explanation.walkthrough: Tommy, or Tommy Atkins, is the nickname for a British private soldier, who in the First World War wore puttees, strips of cloth wound round the lower leg.
explanation.definitionFit: A pane set in place with putty has been puttied, and the word also puns on a soldier dressed in puttees.

clue.text: One we prefer not to have eating at table

definitions.text: One we prefer not to have eating at table

blocks.clueFragment: One we prefer not to have eating at table
blocks.note: surface reading: an unwelcome dinner guest
setter's reading: an insect literally eating into the wooden table

explanation.walkthrough: 'eating at table' sounds like dining; it means gnawing the furniture itself.
explanation.definitionFit: This insect consumes wood, so it is an unwanted pest that devours furniture from within.

clue.text: Conclude that the other one's down?

blocks.note: first meaning: to finish or arrive at last
second meaning, playful: if one end of something is down, the other end must be the raised one

explanation.walkthrough: Think of a seesaw: when one end goes down, the opposite end rises.
explanation.definitionFit: To end up somewhere is to finish there, so the phrasal verb means to conclude.

clue.text: Box and beat the old Greek

blocks.note: to spar is to box in practice
to tan someone's hide is to beat them

explanation.surface: A boxing instruction to fight and defeat an ancient Hellene.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spartan was a citizen of Sparta, a city-state of ancient Greece.

clue.text: Reduced effect of striker in the plant

indicators.note: in puts the striking tool inside the plant's name

blocks.note: a reed is a tall waterside plant
a bat is what strikes the ball in cricket or baseball

explanation.surface: A batsman's blow is softened by landing in the undergrowth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'effect of' only joins the definition to the wordplay; a striker here is the batsman's implement, not a footballer.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebate is an old verb meaning to diminish or deduct, so rebated means lessened.

clue.text: "I have bought Golden s" (Macbeth)

blocks.note: surface reading: a quotation with a word missing
setter's reading: complete Macbeth's line 'I have bought golden ___s from all sorts of people' with the missing word

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank: in Macbeth Act 1 Scene 7 Macbeth says he has won the high regard of everyone, 'golden opinions from all sorts of people'.
explanation.definitionFit: Macbeth's 'golden opinions' are the high esteem and favourable views others hold of him.

clue.text: Lead glittering like Old Glory

blocks.note: the lead in a play or film is its star
spangled means decorated with glittering spangles

explanation.surface: A shiny metal, or a leading actor, sparkling like the flag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' looks like the metal; it is the leading role. Old Glory is a nickname for the United States flag.
explanation.definitionFit: The US flag is studded with stars, hence the anthem title The Star-Spangled Banner.
